Redditch.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Worcestershire
s1loc: Redditch built its visitor draw on an industrial past, and the Forge Mill Needle Museum tells the story of a town that was once the largest needle and fishing-tackle maker in the world, its water-powered machinery still running. Next door the medieval Bordesley Abbey ruins and visitor centre add a Cistercian layer, while the town's New Town heritage and the surrounding Lickey Hills frame a compact but distinctive day-trip offer.

The leisure layer centres on Arrow Valley Country Park, 900 acres of open space wrapped around the 27-acre Arrow Valley Lake, where the Countryside Centre runs watersports, sailing and fishing alongside cafe and conference facilities. A cycleway and bridleway thread the park, and the Millers Trail links walkers from the lake up to Forge Mill, keeping activity operators busy through the warmer months and school holidays.

Culture and events run through the town centre and the Palace Theatre, a restored Edwardian venue staging drama, music and the annual pantomime, with the Kingfisher Shopping Centre anchoring footfall. Heritage walks around the old town and the abbey meadows, plus seasonal markets and festivals, give Redditch a steady cultural calendar that pulls visitors in from Bromsgrove, Studley and the wider Arrow valley.

The visitor trade leans on a mix of business and leisure beds, with hotels and inns serving travellers along the A435 and M42 corridor and the proximity to Birmingham and the NEC. Redditch railway station, the terminus of the Cross-City Line, brings in day-trippers, while tour operators and activity centres tap the green-space draw and the town's position as a base for exploring the Lickey Hills and north Worcestershire countryside.

Harlow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Essex
s1loc: Harlow markets itself as Britain's first Sculpture Town, with an outdoor trail of more than 100 works by Auguste Rodin, Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth scattered across its squares, estates and green spaces. The Gibberd Garden, the Grade II listed home of the town's master planner Sir Frederick Gibberd, adds formal terraces, pools and woodland glades down to Pincey Brook, giving the post-war New Town a genuinely unusual cultural draw.

The leisure and activity layer is anchored by Harlow Town Park, over 160 acres of greenery with Pets Corner, a paddling area and event lawns, plus the Harlow Outdoors centre and the watercourses of the Stort valley. Indoor venues, family attractions and the activity sites around the Pinnacles and Great Parndon keep operators working year-round, with cycling and walking routes linking the town's neighbourhoods to the surrounding Essex countryside.

Heritage and culture run from the Harlow Museum and Walled Gardens, set in a Georgian house with restored kitchen gardens, to the Harlow Playhouse, a two-space theatre staging live music, comedy and an annual pantomime alongside a busy cafe-bar programme. The old village quarters of the town and the listed New Town architecture give heritage walks plenty to point at, supported by a calendar of seasonal markets and festivals.

The visitor trade rests on a solid hotel and serviced-stay base built for business along the M11 and the wider London commuter belt. Harlow Town and Harlow Mill stations on the West Anglia line bring visitors in from London Liverpool Street and Cambridge, while Stansted Airport sits a short hop up the M11, and tour operators and guides tap day-trippers heading on to Bishop's Stortford and the Lee and Stort valleys.

Harrow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north west London
s1loc: Harrow's marquee draw is Harrow School, founded in 1572 by John Lyon and educating Winston Churchill, Lord Byron and a long line of statesmen, its hilltop chapel and Old Schools crowning Harrow-on-the-Hill. Below it, Headstone Manor and Museum sets the borough's local-history collection of more than 15,000 objects around a moated medieval manor house and great tithe barn, spanning Roman finds through to Victorian industry.

The leisure layer spreads across Harrow's green spaces, from Canons Park and its 18th-century parkland to Bentley Priory and Stanmore Common, both Sites of Special Scientific Interest and nature reserves, plus Harrow Recreation Ground and Kenton Recreation Ground for everyday activity. Pinner Memorial Park adds a lake, playgrounds and a cafe, while the wooded ridge offers walking and cycling routes that pull families out across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run from the Bentley Priory Museum, set in the RAF Fighter Command headquarters that ran the Battle of Britain, to the Heath Robinson Museum in Pinner celebrating the illustrator's whimsical inventions. The Harrow Arts Centre in Hatch End programmes theatre, music and community events, while the contrasting characters of grand Harrow-on-the-Hill and bustling Wealdstone give heritage walks and festivals a real local backbone.

The visitor trade benefits from Harrow's place on the edge of the capital, with hotels and serviced stays serving both business and leisure travellers. Harrow-on-the-Hill and Harrow and Wealdstone stations link the Metropolitan line, London Overground and Bakerloo services, and the Warner Bros. Studio Tour at nearby Watford and Wembley's stadium and arena sit minutes away, giving guides and tour operators a strong base for day-trippers across north west London.

St Albans.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Hertfordshire
s1loc: St Albans is one of England's great Roman and medieval cities, its skyline led by St Albans Cathedral, an 11th-century abbey church marking the burial place of Britain's first saint. A short walk away the Verulamium Museum displays some of the finest mosaics outside the Mediterranean and the Sandridge Hoard of Roman gold coins, while the early-13th-century Clock Tower, England's only surviving medieval town belfry, opens its five floors to climbers.

The leisure layer centres on Verulamium Park, over 100 acres of greenery with the River Ver, ornamental lakes, the surviving Roman wall and the Hypocaust, an 1,800-year-old underfloor heating system under cover. Westminster Lodge and its pools, plus the open spaces of Clarence Park and Highfield, keep families and activity operators busy, with walking and cycling routes following the Ver valley and the city's parkland through the season.

Heritage and culture run through the cobbled streets and historic quarters of the city centre, where the St Albans Museum and Gallery, set in the old Town Hall, presents 2,000 years of art and local history. The Alban Arena and the Maltings stage live shows, while the city's medieval coaching inns, the twice-weekly market dating back over a thousand years and a busy festival calendar give heritage tours and events plenty to work with.

The visitor trade is built on a strong base of city-centre hotels, historic inns and Bed and Breakfast stays serving leisure breaks and business alike. St Albans City station puts London St Pancras within around twenty minutes on Thameslink, drawing day-trippers in both directions, while tour operators and guides tap the cathedral, the Roman remains and the easy reach of Hatfield House and the wider Hertfordshire countryside.

Stockton-on-Tees.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Tees Valley
s1loc: Stockton-on-Tees pairs a proud railway and riverside history with a modern waterfront led by the award-winning Infinity Bridge, its twin arches mirrored in the Tees and lit at night. Preston Park Museum and Grounds anchors the heritage draw, a Victorian mansion with a recreated 1895 street, period shops, a walled garden and a Butterfly World tropical house, set in riverside parkland that pulls visitors in from across Teesside.

The activity layer centres on the Tees Barrage and the Tees Barrage International White Water Centre, where managed flows feed kayaking, rafting and powerboating courses alongside an Air Trail high ropes course. The river above the barrage supports rowing, dragonboating and canoeing, and the new Waterfront urban park and riverside paths give families, watersports operators and activity centres a year-round base on the water.

Heritage and culture run from ARC, the town-centre arts centre programming theatre, comedy, music and film, to the restored art deco Stockton Globe, a 3,000-capacity venue that reopened in 2021 to bring touring music and comedy to Teesside. The Stockton International Riverside Festival turns the centre into a free outdoor stage with more than 100 performances, while the historic High Street and market keep the cultural calendar busy.

The visitor trade rests on a hotel base serving business and leisure across the Tees Valley, with the University of Durham's Queen's Campus, the riverside and the town centre drawing event and conference stays. Teesside International Airport sits a short drive away, rail links run through Thornaby and Eaglescliffe, and tour operators tap day-trippers heading on to Middlesbrough, the North York Moors and the Durham coast.

Gosport.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Solent coast
s1loc: Gosport sits across the harbour from Portsmouth with a naval heritage that anchors its visitor draw, led by the Royal Navy Submarine Museum, home to the Cold War boat HMS Alliance, where visitors walk the cramped control room and quarters of the Silent Service. The Explosion Museum of Naval Firepower, set in the 18th-century Priddy's Hard armaments depot, traces torpedoes, missiles and guns across centuries on one of Britain's most important ordnance sites.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the waterfront, with Stokes Bay and its shingle seafront, sailing and watersports drawing families through the summer, and Walpole Park and the Gosport coastal path linking the foreshore. Lee-on-the-Solent nearby adds a long promenade and beach, while marinas and dinghy clubs around Haslar and the harbour give watersports operators and activity centres a busy seasonal base on the Solent.

Heritage and culture build on the harbour itself, where the Gosport Heritage Trail links Holy Trinity Church, the old fortifications and the historic Royal Hospital Haslar, while the restored Falkland Gardens and the waterfront frame the town's events. The annual seafront and harbour festivals, the Diving Museum at Stokes Bay and a calendar of maritime events give guides and culture operators a distinctly naval story to tell.

The visitor trade leans on its tight link to Portsmouth, with the Gosport Ferry and a waterbus running across the harbour to the Historic Dockyard, HMS Victory and the Mary Rose. A hotel and Bed and Breakfast base serves leisure and naval-business stays, while road links along the A32 and the wider Solent draw bring day-trippers, and tour operators tap visitors heading on to Fareham, Lee-on-the-Solent and the Isle of Wight ferries.

Scunthorpe.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of North Lincolnshire
s1loc: Scunthorpe anchors North Lincolnshire's visitor offer, with Normanby Hall Country Park the marquee draw, a 300-acre estate around a Regency mansion built in the 1820s by Sir Robert Smirke, complete with a restored Victorian walled garden, a deer park and a Farming Museum of Lincolnshire agricultural heritage. The North Lincolnshire Museum in the town carries the story from prehistory and Roman finds through to the steel industry that built modern Scunthorpe.

The leisure layer centres on Central Park, a large urban green space with gardens, play areas, a splash pad and cafe, while the surrounding country parks and golf courses give families and activity operators room across the season. Normanby Hall's woodland trails, ornamental ponds and seasonal events draw visitors out into the estate, and the wider North Lincolnshire countryside and the Humber bank add walking and cycling routes for day-trippers.

Heritage and culture run from the 20-21 Visual Arts Centre, a contemporary gallery set in a former church staging a rotating programme of art and craft exhibitions, workshops and free creative activities, to the Plowright Theatre staging drama, music and pantomime. The town's steel-making story, the markets and a calendar of seasonal events give heritage and culture operators a distinctly industrial-Lincolnshire backbone to work with.

The visitor trade rests on a hotel and serviced-stay base serving both business and leisure across North Lincolnshire, with Scunthorpe's steelworks history and its position near the Humber drawing trade and event stays. Scunthorpe station links the line between Doncaster and Cleethorpes, Humberside Airport sits a short drive away, and tour operators tap day-trippers heading on to Gainsborough, the Humber bridge and the Lincolnshire coast.
